cards.explanation: The answer is the top of the cedar. Verse 3 says the eagle “…came to Lebanon and took away the top of the cedar.” Not a branch, not a few leaves, the top. He walked in like he owned the place, and I'm not sure he even looked around first.

The answer is in fertile soil by abundant waters, friends. Verse 5 says the eagle “…planted it in fertile soil…” and “…placed it by abundant waters…” That's the seed of the land, a separate planting from the cedar's shoot. Good dirt and plenty of water is about the best setup a plant can ask for.
The answer is False. There's no tower here. Verse 6 says it “…sprouted and became a spreading vine, low in height…” It spreads instead of standing tall.

The answer is toward the eagle who planted it, friends. Verse 6 says the vine had “…branches turned toward him…” and the him is the eagle who planted it. At this point in the riddle, the vine leans toward that first eagle. Verse 7 will bring another eagle into the picture.

The answer is True. Verse 7 says that when the second eagle appears, “…this vine bent its roots toward him.” Back in verse 6, its roots remained where it stood, so this is a shift. A new eagle walks in and this vine swivels like somebody who just heard their name called.

The answer is water. Verse 7 says the vine stretched out its branches to him “…so that he might water it.” It's reaching for a drink. Verse 8 says it was already planted in good soil by abundant waters, so I think it's reaching past what it already had.

The answer is that it will be uprooted and wither. God asks, “Will it not be uprooted and stripped of its fruit so that it shrivels?” and says, “All its foliage will wither!” (verse 9). Reaching for the second eagle doesn't pay off for this vine. It isn't going to come out of this well.
The answer is False. Verse 9 says, “It will not take a strong arm or many people to pull it up by its roots.” God isn't describing a tough job. No heavy lifting required.

The answer is the east wind. Verse 10 asks, “Will it not completely wither when the east wind strikes?” Even if the vine moves somewhere new, that wind is still coming. The verse ends by saying it will wither “…on the bed where it sprouted.”

The answer is the king of Babylon, friends. Verse 12 says, “…the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, carried off its king and officials, and brought them back with him to Babylon.” This is God explaining what the riddle's things mean. Jerusalem's king and officials are the ones carried off.

The answer is that he makes a covenant with him under oath. Verse 13 says the king of Babylon “…made a covenant with him, putting him under oath.” An oath is a serious promise, and this one has a covenant behind it. The same verse goes on to say he carried away the leading men of the land.

The answer is False. Verse 14 says it was “…so that the kingdom would be brought low, unable to lift itself up, surviving only by keeping his covenant.” That's a kingdom with no way to stand on its own. Its only way to survive is keeping the covenant.
The answer is Egypt. Verse 15 says this king rebelled “…by sending his envoys to Egypt…” An envoy is someone sent to carry a message. That's how he rebelled against Babylon.

The answer is horses and a large army, friends. Verse 15 says the king sent envoys to Egypt “…to ask for horses and a large army.” He's shopping for muscle. Right after, the verse asks, “Will he flourish?”

The answer is True. In verse 16, God declares that “he will die in Babylon, in the land of the king who enthroned him, whose oath he despised and whose covenant he broke.” Verse 15 had asked, “Can he break a covenant and yet escape?” This is the answer. He doesn't escape the king he rebelled against.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says, “Pharaoh with his mighty army and vast horde will not help him in battle…” Pharaoh, king of Egypt, has the mighty army, and God says it will not help this king in battle. A big army doesn't count for much when God has said it won't help.

The answer is the treason he committed against God, friends. God says He will “…bring him to Babylon and execute judgment upon him there for the treason he committed against Me.” (verse 20). The text names this as the reason. The treason is against God.

The answer is that they are scattered to every wind. Verse 21 says, “…those who survive will be scattered to every wind.” I think this part is heavy, friends. The verse ends with God saying that then they will know He is the LORD.

The answer is the LORD Himself. In verse 22 the Lord GOD says, “I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out.” Back in verse 3, it was an eagle who took the top of the cedar. This time the one who does the taking is God.

The answer is on the mountain heights of Israel, friends. The LORD says, “I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel so that it will bear branches…” (verse 23). Verse 22 calls the place “…a high and lofty mountain.” It's planted in Israel's high places.
The answer is cedar. Verse 23 says it will “…bear branches; it will yield fruit and become a majestic cedar.” Verse 22 called it “…a tender sprig…” So it goes from a tender sprig to a majestic cedar.
The answer is False. Verse 23 says, “Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches.” Every kind of bird is welcome. Eagles aren't the only guests.

The answer is that God makes it tall, friends. God says in verse 24, “I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall.” The tall one comes down and the low one goes up. That's the LORD turning the order upside down.

The answer is True. God says in verse 24, “I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish.” God dries up the green one, and the withered one gets to flourish. It comes right after “I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall.”
